A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same hierarchical dynamical systems reconstruction work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A and B are readable and support reliable comparison across relocations and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction, transfer-learning, feature-regression, and clustering experiments on dynamical-system benchmarks, simulated arterial pulse waves, EEG, and fMRI data.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds architecture comparisons, stability and computational analyses, nonstationary and mixed-system experiments, and electricity-load results.

M1.justification: The core hierarchy, linear feature-to-parameter mapping, shPLRNN, and GTF training remain. v2 adds a proof-of-concept extension in which a jointly trained MLP maps subject features and time to time-dependent model parameters (Section 4.2, Figure 16). It also instantiates the hierarchy with a Markov Neural Operator trained using prediction and dissipative losses (Appendix A.5.1). These are bounded extensions of the existing framework.

E1.justification: v2 adds electricity-load data from 370 sites, including clustering and one-day forecasting; joint training across Lorenz-63, Rössler, and newly included Chua systems; and a nonstationary Lorenz scenario with drifting control parameters (Figures 16, 27–28). These extend the domains and dynamical conditions beyond v1's retained benchmarks and biomedical applications.

E2.justification: The original CoDA, LEADS, shPLRNN-ensemble, and EEG comparator sets remain. v2 adds ensemble-versus-hierarchical vanilla RNN and LSTM comparisons (Table 3), plus a separate comparison of shPLRNN against N-HITS, Transformers, and Temporal Convolutional Networks (Figure 29). These substantially broaden the evaluated alternatives; the hierarchical Markov Neural Operator is an adaptation, not a competing baseline.

E3.justification: New protocols include joint sweeps of subject count and trajectory length, timing with 20,000 total observations held constant, and forecasting comparisons using 500 training epochs, 100-step input windows, 30-step forecasts, and long-term autocorrelations (Figures 13–14, 29). Appendix A.3 also changes the stated simulator from fourth-order Runge–Kutta to odeint/LSODA. The EEG GMM repetition description changes as well. These reported revisions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds cross-run feature-space stability analyses across datasets, alternative recurrent architectures and observation-model ablations, subject-count scaling, computational-cost analyses, and a nonstationary case study (Appendices A.1.5–A.1.9; Figure 16). These address robustness, component dependence, and scalability beyond v1's existing batching, feature-count, hierarchization, and trajectory-length analyses.

E5.justification: v1's EEG Table 5 states that ten randomly initialized GMMs were evaluated per training run; v2's Table 7 specifies one GMM per run and explains the sources of variation. v2 also explicitly reports SEM across ten runs for convergence timing (Figure 14). Existing median/MAD, standard-deviation, and one-sided t-test reporting largely remains. The PDFs do not establish whether the EEG repetition change reflects rerunning or corrected documentation.

E6.justification: v2 adds architecture scores, feature-stability correlations, scaling and timing results, nonstationary and mixed-system reconstructions, electricity forecasts, and Markov Neural Operator parameter recovery with R² = 0.97 (Figure 18). Main Table 1 and EEG accuracy values remain unchanged. Existing ablation p-values change: for example, outer-product state-divergence p changes from 16% to 0.84, and MLP p-values from 100% to 0.0, despite unchanged performance summaries and t-statistics (v1 Table 2; v2 Table 4).

T1.justification: Equation 5 corrects the stated Gaussian loss: v1 has negative terms and an M/2 log-determinant coefficient, while v2 uses positive half-weighted terms summed over subjects and time. Appendix A.4 also revises CoDA's formal description from additive dynamics to hypernetwork-generated parameters. These are mathematical corrections; no substantial new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The central claims about generative reconstruction, interpretable features, and transfer/few-shot learning remain. v2's conclusion explicitly extends the information-sharing claim to systems governed by different equations. The foundation-model perspective becomes more prominent in the abstract, but was already present in v1's conclusion.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for faster convergence with more subjects and for architecture/observation-model behavior. Its limitations emphasize comparable time scales, the preliminary nature of the nonstationary extension, and difficulties constructing physical priors across domains. This replaces v1's emphasis on untested generality, using available class labels, and Bayesian posterior uncertainty, substantially revising the applicability discussion.

D1.justification: v2 reports a public GitHub repository instead of anonymous code with a promised future release. It adds hyperparameter-selection details, fMRI region extraction information, electricity preprocessing and delay embedding, Markov Neural Operator training details, and hardware/configurations for timing experiments. These materially expand reproducibility documentation; the repository's actual availability was not externally checked.

R1.justification: v2 adds targeted discussion of switching/decomposed dynamical systems, LFADS, and CrEIMBO, alongside references supporting the new architectures and datasets. It removes several foundation-model, Bayesian-modeling, and clinical-background citations. The principal positioning around generative reconstruction across dynamical regimes remains, so this is a focused update rather than a fundamental repositioning.

P1.justification: v2 substantially condenses the introduction, reorganizes the methods around the hierarchical model and explicit total loss, moves initialization and learning-rate explanations into dedicated appendix subsections, and rewrites the limitations. These changes alter the explanatory structure beyond adding experimental content. The publication header and affiliations also change.

P2.justification: The framework schematic moves from v1 Appendix Figure 7 to v2 main-text Figure 1, and a separate training-flow diagram is added. New tables and multipanel figures display stability, architecture comparisons, scaling, computation, nonstationarity, electricity, mixed systems, and forecasting comparisons. Several retained plots receive revised axes, colorbars, or captions; most original figures remain through renumbering.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1's support for the framework's generality and reliability through architecture ablations, cross-run stability analysis, mixed-system and nonstationary tests, and controlled computational studies. The corrected loss formulation and expanded implementation documentation also improve reproducibility. The main performance scores remain unchanged. Unexplained revisions to existing p-values and GMM repetition descriptions leave localized reporting uncertainty, but the broader validation provides a substantial net quality improvement.
